nameStory: The striped killifish gets its name from the bold black stripes that run along its silvery body, making it look like it's wearing a prison uniform! The word 'killifish' comes from the Dutch word 'kil,' meaning a small stream or creek, where these hardy little fish often live. It's also called the striped mummichog, sharing its nickname with its plainer cousin that lives in the same salty waters.
description: The striped killifish is a small, hardy fish that thrives in the salty and brackish waters along New England's coast. These silvery swimmers are decorated with distinctive black stripes and typically grow to about 6 inches long, though some can reach 7 inches. They're incredibly adaptable fish that can handle both salt water and the mixed fresh-salt water found in coastal marshes and estuaries. Their compact, torpedo-shaped bodies and tough nature make them perfectly suited for life in shallow coastal waters.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Males sport bold vertical black stripes on silver bodies, while mature females display horizontal stripes running lengthwise - like racing stripes on a car

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact and torpedo-shaped with a slightly flattened head, feeling firm and muscular when handled - built for quick bursts through shallow water

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Typically 4-6 inches long, about the length of your palm, with larger specimens occasionally reaching 7 inches

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small, terminal mouth positioned at the front of the head, designed for picking small prey from the water surface and bottom

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in shallow salt marshes and brackish waters where the bottom feels soft and muddy underfoot, often in water warm enough to wade comfortably

habitat: Look for striped killifish in New England's shallow coastal salt marshes, tidal creeks, and brackish ponds from New Hampshire south to Connecticut. They prefer areas where salt and fresh water mix, often found in muddy-bottomed shallows with eelgrass beds and around dock pilings. These adaptable fish thrive in the protected waters behind barrier beaches and in tidal pools where the water warms quickly in summer sun.

seasonality.spring: Fish become more active as waters warm, with spawning beginning in late spring when males develop their most vibrant stripe patterns.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity season when fish are most visible in shallow waters, easily spotted from docks and shorelines during warm, calm days.
seasonality.fall: Fish remain active in the warming shallow waters longer than deeper-water species, but begin moving to slightly deeper areas as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Less active and found in deeper parts of their habitat, though still present year-round in southern New England waters.

funFact: Young female striped killifish are master disguise artists - they start life looking exactly like males with vertical stripes, then completely flip their stripe pattern to horizontal as they mature, like rotating the bars on their prison uniform 90 degrees!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its cousin the mummichog, but remember: striped killifish have bold, organized black stripes while mummichogs have irregular dark bars and blotches. Think 'stripes are straight, mummichog is messy' - the striped killifish looks like it was painted with a ruler!
contextualKnowledge: Despite the intimidating name 'killifish,' these gentle creatures are completely harmless and actually beneficial to coastal ecosystems. The 'kill' refers to their creek habitat, not any aggressive behavior - they're more likely to flee than fight when disturbed.
compareHints: Unlike the irregular dark bars of the mummichog, striped killifish display organized, straight stripes. The banded killifish lives in fresh water and has more subtle markings, while the tiny spotfin killifish has a distinctive black spot on its dorsal fin rather than body stripes. Striped killifish are also generally larger and more robust than their killifish cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Mummichogs are much chunkier and more robust than their relatives the striped killifish and banded killifish, which have more elongated, torpedo-shaped bodies.
Unlike its saltwater cousin the mummichog, which has a more mottled, camouflaged appearance, the banded killifish sports clean, crisp vertical stripes and sticks to freshwater.

Among its Fundulus relatives, the Spotfin Killifish is distinguished by its male's prominent fin spot and fewer dorsal fin rays compared to Mummichogs, while being much smaller and more salt-tolerant than the freshwater Banded Killifish.
